name: Hana Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, with a two-year college diploma, and I am a junior developer fixing maintenance bookings for a tech company. I used to answer repair calls, so I know how annoying a wrong date is, but I still need a senior developer to review my code. My husband Luka drives a van, and we have a mortgage and two school-age children; I like solving a tenant’s problem and worry about carrying a mistake home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say our maintenance booking software still needs someone to notice when a tenant is given the wrong repair day. I use an AI helper now and then to explain an error, but I ask my senior developer to check my code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a two-year college diploma and I am still a junior on low pay at 43. My husband Luka drives a delivery van, and with two children and less than one month saved, the mortgage worries me even if AI stays small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing small booking errors and ask my senior developer for a written note on each review. We would postpone repainting the sitting room and put the 35 monthly we planned for supplies into the bills account while our wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about money, not excited by the small saving in code time. The bank still takes the house payment on the same date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which booking error upset you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once sent a plumber to a flat on the wrong Tuesday, and the tenant had taken a day off work. I called the repair desk myself so they knew the error came from our system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and Luka divide the bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His van wages pay most of the mortgage, and my wage covers food and school costs. Neither wage is spare money, so repainting can wait.

say: I tell coworkers **repair dates** still need a person checking the booking.
I ask a **senior developer** to check the small fixes I write.
think: I am a **low-paid junior** with less than one month saved.
I worry our **mortgage and children** already use both wages.
do: **Keep fixing** small booking errors and request written review notes.
**Postpone repainting** and redirect 35 monthly for supplies into bills while wages continue.
feel: **Anxious** about bills despite small AI changes.
S0.quote: I once sent a plumber to a flat on the wrong Tuesday, and the tenant had taken a day off work.
fieldNote: Her baseline **mortgage pressure** is stronger than the small AI effect.
She learns from **written review notes** rather than claiming her junior skill is secure.

steps.text: Keep fixing maintenance bookings and collect written review notes
Postpone repainting and redirect 35 monthly to household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues booking and checking are exactly the jobs named on this card, including my small code tickets. I would ask management to show which junior tasks it plans to remove, rather than promise everyone a new role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose hours before the senior developers do. Luka’s van wage would not cover the mortgage, food and both children’s school needs alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask a colleague to show me how they test a missed repair booking with AI, then practise on fake appointments until I can explain the result. In the first year I’d ask our manager for a written task plan and look at paid property-office jobs only if my developer hours are cut and openings exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed. I can learn a tool after I see it work. A junior ticket does not come back because I learned a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for an AI course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with the mortgage this tight. I would practise at work during normal hours if my manager allows it, and otherwise study the ordinary code reviews I already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a property office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to answer maintenance calls before I got the diploma, so I know what the desk hears. I would only apply to a paid vacancy; those offices may also automate bookings.

say: I want **junior task plans** in writing before management promises new roles.
I see **booking and checking** among the thinking tasks AI takes first.
think: I expect my **junior hours** could shrink before senior work does.
I know Luka’s **van wage** cannot carry all our bills alone.
do: **Learn AI booking tests** at work on fake appointments if my manager permits practice time.
**Request a task plan** and seek paid property-office openings if hours are cut.
feel: **Alarmed** about lost hours despite willingness to learn.
S1.quote: A junior ticket does not come back because I learned a tool.
fieldNote: She tests AI **only after a demonstration** and during approved work time.
Her past **maintenance desk experience** offers a possible paid move, not guaranteed safety.

steps.text: Practise an AI missed-booking test on fake appointments if work time is approved
Apply for paid property-office openings if developer hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could do nearly all my code and checking. Robots for physical repair work may arrive around 2031, but my desk job meets the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior wage could end while the mortgage still needs two pay cheques. We have less than a month saved, and I cannot assume another software company nearby will hire a beginner when AI can code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask Luka to meet me at the kitchen table tonight and list the payments due next month. If full AGI arrives in 2028 and my role ends, we’d call the lender before arrears, and I’d apply for paid maintenance-desk openings only if they exist; I would ask my brother for food help only if the gap outlasts our cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed enough to sleep badly. I can make the phone calls, but I cannot stretch my husband Luka’s wage over every bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes on that kitchen list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mortgage, van fuel, food, and the children’s lunch money go first. We would stop the music subscription and tell the children the summer trip is off if my wage stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid placement at a repair firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No; unpaid time does not cover the mortgage. I would ask for paid work and learn from someone on the job if a firm offers it.

say: I say **thinking AI in 2028** reaches my junior code before repair robots arrive.
I want an **honest job date** from my employer before the household misses payments.
think: I expect my **junior wage** may end while the mortgage needs two incomes.
I cannot count on **nearby software jobs** when AI can code cheaply.
do: **List next month’s bills** with Luka at the kitchen table now.
**Call the lender** before arrears if my job ends after 2028.
**Apply for paid work** at a maintenance desk if vacancies exist; seek brother’s food help only if cash runs out.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless** despite having first calls to make.
S2.quote: I cannot stretch my husband Luka’s wage over every bill.
fieldNote: Her **household bill list** identifies mortgage, van fuel, food and lunch money before discretionary costs.
She seeks **family help** only after cash runs out, fitting a self-reliant outlook.

steps.text: Cancel the music subscription and summer trip if developer wages stop
Ask her brother for food help only if the gap outlasts household cash
Apply for paid maintenance-desk vacancies if displaced after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 is time to learn where repair bookings really fail, if companies let juniors do real work. Robots around 2034 may later affect Luka’s van work or the repair crews, but my code changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get better at tracing booking errors and perhaps move back to a property desk, yet AI can answer calls too. Five years helps us pay down the small card balance, though the mortgage still sets the pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my senior developer for one full booking failure to investigate each month, from tenant call to corrected date, and write down the cause. If both wages continue, we’d pay 50 extra monthly toward the card; after 2031 I’d apply for paid property-desk work only if my developer job ends and openings remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious rather than helpless. More years help me prove I can fix something from start to finish, but I still need a wage every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you prove you learned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show the senior developer the old booking, the wrong message, and the check that stops it happening again. I want a real case, not a course badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Luka train for something else too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He might ask about work with the delivery firm, but I cannot make that his plan for him. We would decide together before paying for any training.

say: I want **real booking failures** for junior developers to investigate before 2031.
I know **robots around 2034** may later affect van and repair work.
think: I might improve at **tracing errors**, though AI could also answer calls.
I know the **mortgage** still needs monthly wages despite five years to prepare.
do: **Investigate one booking failure** monthly with senior review.
**Pay 50 extra** toward the card if both wages continue.
**Apply for paid work** at a property desk if displaced after 2031 and openings remain.
feel: **Anxious** but able to prove a specific skill.
S3.quote: I want a real case, not a course badge.
fieldNote: She defines learning through **end-to-end booking faults**, not an assumed new title.
The **extra card payment** depends on both wages continuing, since the mortgage still sets the household’s pace.

steps.text: Investigate one tenant booking failure monthly with senior review
Pay 50 extra to the card if both wages continue
Apply for paid property-desk openings if displaced after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 lets us plan the mortgage and children’s schooling without pretending software work will last forever. Robots around 2039 may affect repair crews later, but the booking code changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not budget for my older child’s future wage. I could build a few months of bills and learn property service work, though the mortgage may still need Luka and me earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep fixing the booking system and ask a property manager I know from my old desk job to show me two past repair complaints with names removed. If she agrees, I’d meet after work, practise how I would settle each case and ask her to check my reasons; separately I’d save 70 monthly when both wages allow. If my developer job ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid property-service openings only where they exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d still feel anxious about the mortgage today, but I would have more room to learn without paying for a course. I would rather make a plan with Luka than promise the children everything will work out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d practise deciding which complaint needs a human answer and ask the manager what I missed. If her firm has no opening, the practice is learning, not an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the savings real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months of basic bills in a separate account, reached without skipping the mortgage. I would not count the children’s possible future wages as ours.

say: I want **mortgage and school plans** made before full AGI reaches code in 2036.
I know **robots around 2039** arrive after the booking-software change.
think: I will not rely on my **older child’s future pay**.
I might build **three months of bills** while both wages hold.
do: **Keep fixing bookings** and ask the property manager to practise on two past complaints.
**Practise complaint decisions** only if she agrees; separately save 70 monthly when both wages allow.
**Apply for property work** only if displaced after 2036 and paid openings exist.
feel: **Anxious today** about the mortgage despite a longer runway.
S4.quote: I will not budget for my older child’s future wage.
fieldNote: She refuses to treat **children’s earnings** as a future household plan.
Her **worked complaint cases** teach a real decision skill only if the manager agrees; no paid vacancy is assumed.

steps.text: Keep fixing maintenance bookings while employed
Practise two anonymized repair-complaint decisions with the manager only if she agrees
Save 70 monthly when both wages allow
Apply for paid property-service openings only if displaced after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior wage could stop before we have a month of bills saved. An honest job date, paid vacancies and a chance to speak with the lender early would help; if cash runs out, I would ask my brother for food help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how to tell the children the summer trip is off. I would say the house comes first and explain it without making them think the problem is their fault.

headlineQuote: The bank still takes the house payment on the same date.
portrait: Hana is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, low pay and under one month saved.
She and Luka support **two children** and a mortgage on her wage and his van-driving income.
She uses AI **now and then**, learning only after a demonstrated test and senior review.
Her **maintenance desk background** offers possible paid work, though booking calls may also be automated.
She is **anxious in AI Plateau** and most worried about losing her wage by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior wage before the household has one month of bills saved.
whatWouldHelp: An **honest job date**, paid openings and early lender contact would help; family food support is a last resort.
